description:
We’re a team of six from Amman, Jordan, mostly Computer Engineering students at German Jordanian University. We’re passionate about technology, AI, and space, and we’re excited to use NASA data to build something meaningful.

Our team brings together skills in programming, data analysis, web development, and design.

Our team is currently full and we’re not looking for new members. Good luck to everyone this year

We’re tackling Flame in Freefall
summary:
We built an AI research assistant for fire in space. Ask a question in plain English and it answers using only NASA's own microgravity combustion data, citing the exact paper and page for every fact. If the data doesn't answer the question, it says so instead of guessing.

It addresses the challenge by turning NASA's scattered PSI experiments, test tables and papers into one searchable source. Users can pick a habitat atmosphere, such as a Moon base, Mars transit or the ISS, and see which real NASA fire tests match those oxygen and pressure conditions, on a dashboard, a parameter map and an interactive 3D view. Answers can also show the real story behind the data, like Apollo 1 or the Mir fire.

This matters because future Moon and Mars habitats will use richer oxygen at lower pressure, where materials burn more easily. Engineers designing them need fast, trustworthy answers from real test data, not guesses.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Afterburn is a web app for the Flame in Freefall challenge that explores NASA's microgravity combustion research. It has three parts:

• Chat: ask any question about fire in space. Answers are written only from NASA documents and data, with a numbered citation on every fact. Hovering a number shows the exact paper and page. Questions that are off topic, or that the data can't answer, are refused instead of guessed. Some answers offer a "Why this matters" story (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, the 1997 Mir fire, NASA spinoffs), each from a NASA source.

• Dashboard: pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars transit) or set oxygen and pressure with sliders. The app ranks the real Saffire spacecraft fire tests closest to that atmosphere and explains the score. Tabs show a parameter map, plots, the full test data, extracted findings and side by side comparisons, plus a search bar for tests, experiments and findings.

• 3D view: every Saffire test placed by oxygen, pressure and peak carbon monoxide, to explore in 3D.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: we merged NASA PSI's 22 combustion test tables (each with different columns and units) into one clean table: 2,016 rows, 263 standardized columns with units, 1,951 usable tests, 49 duplicates marked, and 13 suspect values flagged instead of silently changed. A document parser extracted 891 findings from 33 NASA documents, and every finding's quote was checked against the source text. Only the 778 verified findings are used.

2. Retrieval (RAG): PDFs, Word files, spreadsheets and tables are split into about 5,000 passages. Search combines keyword search (BM25) and meaning search (bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings), boosts passages about the experiment or test named in the question, reranks the best 30 with a cross encoder (ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2), and keeps a variety of sources.

3. Answering: an LLM writes the answer under strict rules: use only the given passages, cite every sentence, copy numbers exactly, keep microgravity and Earth gravity results separate, and never present Moon or Mars values as measured. It works with any OpenAI compatible LLM API, so the model can be swapped by changing one settings file (our demo uses Google Gemini). Fake citations are removed automatically, and a coverage check refuses unrelated questions before any AI call.

4. Evaluation: we measured retrieval with test questions. The correct passage was ranked first in 21 of 30 questions (28 of 30 in the top 6), and 14 of 20 on held out questions we never tuned for (17 of 20 in the top 6). All unrelated questions were refused.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Spacecraft fire safety engineers, materials engineers and habitat designers can get answers from decades of NASA fire research in seconds, with every claim traceable to its source. Future Moon and Mars habitats are planned with lower pressure and more oxygen, where materials burn more easily, and NASA has very little partial gravity fire data, so the app shows where the data is and where the gaps are. It also helps students learn microgravity combustion from real data.

CREATIVITY

A trustworthy AI that refuses rather than guesses, habitat atmospheres matched to real tests, a 3D map of NASA's fire tests, and real stories connected to the data. The background flame changes between "In Space" (a dim blue ball) and "On Earth" (a teardrop) and reacts to the chosen oxygen and pressure.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Trust and verification (citations, verified quotes, refusals), keeping 0 g, 1 g and partial gravity results separate, data quality (units, duplicates, flagged values), and free tools so anyone can run it.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, sentence-transformers, PyMuPDF, python docx, openpyxl, NumPy, pandas, Pydantic, LiteLLM, any OpenAI compatible LLM API (Google Gemini in our demo), JavaScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, Recharts, Motion and Lucide icons.
